prompt: Suppose the experimenters wanted to test whether the volume of hydrogen peroxide affects the time for the reaction to finish. Which change to the procedure of Experiment 1 would best test this?

choices.text: Measure the volume of hydrogen peroxide in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the time for the reaction to finish
choices.rationale: Measuring the volume of hydrogen peroxide does not test its effect; it must be deliberately varied.

choices.text: Vary the volume of hydrogen peroxide while holding the mass of catalyst and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

choices.text: Vary both the volume of hydrogen peroxide and the mass of catalyst at the same time in each trial, measuring the time for the reaction to finish
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the mass of catalyst
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about catalyst mass but never changes the volume of hydrogen peroxide.

explanation: A fair test of the volume of hydrogen peroxide changes it alone. The mass of catalyst, which was the variable in Experiment 1, must now be held fixed.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students mixed 50 mL of hydrogen peroxide solution from a single bottle with a measured mass of powdered catalyst and timed how long it took for the bubbling to stop. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: A student claims that the temperature of the solution affects the time for the reaction to finish. Do the results of Experiments 1 and 2 support this claim?

choices.text: No; the two experiments gave the same reaction time at every catalyst mass tested
choices.rationale: The columns differ at every catalyst mass; compare them row by row.

choices.text: No; the time for the reaction to finish decreased as catalyst mass increased in both experiments
choices.rationale: A shared trend with catalyst mass says nothing about whether the temperature of the solution matters; the two columns differ at every row.

choices.text: Yes; at every catalyst mass tested, the time for the reaction to finish was higher for 20°C than for 30°C
choices.rationale: Correct. The two experiments differ only in this condition, and the results differ consistently between them.

choices.text: Yes; the time for the reaction to finish decreased as catalyst mass increased in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2
choices.rationale: That trend concerns catalyst mass, not the temperature of the solution; it would appear even if the condition had no effect.

explanation: Because the experiments differ only in the temperature of the solution, the consistent gap between the two sets of results (higher for 20°C) shows that the condition affects the time for the reaction to finish.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students mixed 50 mL of hydrogen peroxide solution from a single bottle with a measured mass of powdered catalyst in a water bath at 20°C and timed how long it took for the bubbling to stop. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated in a water bath at 30°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: To decide whether the type of meal has an effect on the blood glucose level, a student should compare the results of:

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the type of meal
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the time after the meal under one condition
choices.rationale: Experiment 1 used a single setting of the type of meal, so by itself it cannot reveal its effect.

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the time after the meal was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying time in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed consisting of whole-grain bread with the same number of calories
choices.rationale: Experiment 2 also used only one setting of the type of meal; a comparison is required.

explanation: Each experiment holds the type of meal fixed at one setting; the two settings differ between experiments, so comparing Experiments 1 and 2 isolates its effect.

stimulus.title: Blood Glucose After a Meal
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A volunteer ate a measured meal consisting of a sugary drink after fasting overnight. A small blood sample was taken at set times afterward and its glucose concentration measured with a glucose meter.
Results (the blood glucose level): at 15 min, 137 mg/dL; at 30 min, 158 mg/dL; at 45 min, 161 mg/dL; at 60 min, 154 mg/dL; at 90 min, 133 mg/dL.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated consisting of whole-grain bread with the same number of calories, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 15 min, 116 mg/dL; at 30 min, 129 mg/dL; at 45 min, 131 mg/dL; at 60 min, 127 mg/dL; at 90 min, 114 mg/dL.

prompt: Suppose Experiment 1 were repeated with a tray temperature of 20°C, a setting between those used in Experiments 1 and 2. At a soaking time of 4 h, the percent of seeds that sprouted would most likely be:

choices.text: between 55% and 77%
choices.rationale: These are the results for 8 h, not 4 h.

choices.text: above both experiments' results, greater than 56%
choices.rationale: This is above both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: below both experiments' results, less than 40%
choices.rationale: This is below both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: between 40% and 56%
choices.rationale: Correct. At 4 h, Experiment 1 gave 40 and Experiment 2 gave 56; an intermediate setting should give an intermediate result.

explanation: The two experiments bracket the new setting, so the result at 4 h should lie between 40 and 56 %.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students soaked batches of 50 radish seeds in water for a set number of hours, then placed each batch on damp paper towels in a covered tray and kept the trays at 15°C. After 5 days they counted the seeds that had sprouted and converted the count to a percent. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated and kept the trays at 25°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which of the following is the most serious flaw in the procedure of Experiment 1?

choices.text: The reaction time changed between trials, confounding the effect of the pH of the solution
choices.rationale: Correct. A second factor that changes along with the independent variable confounds the results.

choices.text: The activity of the enzyme was measured in every trial rather than only in the final trial of the series
choices.rationale: The dependent variable must be measured in every trial.

choices.text: Only a single value of the pH of the solution was tested, so no trend could possibly be identified
choices.rationale: The results list 6 different values of pH.

choices.text: The pH of the solution was deliberately changed from trial to trial instead of being held constant throughout
choices.rationale: Changing the independent variable is the point of the experiment, not a flaw.

explanation: Good design changes only pH. Because the reaction time also changed, any difference in enzyme activity could be due to either factor.

stimulus.title: Enzyme Activity and pH
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students added 1 mL of enzyme solution to tubes containing a substrate solution buffered to a set pH. They measured how much product formed in 5 minutes to find the activity. Each pH was tested in triplicate. The experimenters did not keep the reaction time the same from one trial to the next.
Results (the activity of the enzyme): at pH 3, 4 µmol/min; at pH 4, 19 µmol/min; at pH 5, 44 µmol/min; at pH 6, 51 µmol/min; at pH 7, 29 µmol/min; at pH 8, 8 µmol/min.

prompt: Which of the following conclusions is NOT supported by the results of Experiment 1?

choices.text: The mass of yeast has no effect on the volume of carbon dioxide produced.
choices.rationale: Correct. The mass of yeast was held constant, so the experiment provides no evidence about its effect.

choices.text: The volume of carbon dioxide produced was greater at 6 g than at 0 g.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The volume of carbon dioxide produced was greater at 10 g than at 0 g.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The volume of carbon dioxide produced was greater at 10 g than at 4 g.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

explanation: Three of the statements can be checked against the table and hold. "The mass of yeast has no effect on the volume of carbon dioxide produced." cannot: the mass of yeast was held constant, so the experiment provides no evidence about its effect.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students mixed 5 g of dry yeast with 100 mL of warm water and a measured mass of sugar in a bottle. A balloon over the bottle's mouth collected the gas, and after 30 minutes the volume of carbon dioxide was measured. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: Suppose the experimenters wanted to test whether the car used affects the fuel efficiency. Which change to the procedure of Experiment 1 would best test this?

choices.text: Vary both the car used and the steady speed of the car at the same time in each trial, measuring the fuel efficiency
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Measure the car used in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the fuel efficiency
choices.rationale: Measuring the car used does not test its effect; it must be deliberately varied.

choices.text: Vary the car used while holding the steady speed of the car and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the steady speed of the car
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about speed but never changes the car used.

explanation: A fair test of the car used changes it alone. The steady speed of the car, which was the variable in Experiment 1, must now be held fixed.

table.caption: Experiment 1: A test driver drove the same car around a flat track at a steady speed for 20 km and measured the fuel used. Fuel efficiency was calculated as kilometers traveled per liter of fuel. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: Based on Experiments 1 and 2, is the claim that the streambed type affects the number of mayfly nymphs supported?

choices.text: Yes; the number of mayfly nymphs increased as dissolved oxygen increased in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2
choices.rationale: That trend concerns dissolved oxygen, not the streambed type; it would appear even if the condition had no effect.

choices.text: Yes; at every dissolved oxygen tested, the number of mayfly nymphs was higher for gravel bed than for sand bed
choices.rationale: Correct. The two experiments differ only in this condition, and the results differ consistently between them.

choices.text: No; the number of mayfly nymphs increased as dissolved oxygen increased in both experiments
choices.rationale: A shared trend with dissolved oxygen says nothing about whether the streambed type matters; the two columns differ at every row.

choices.text: No; the two experiments gave the same mayfly count at every dissolved oxygen tested
choices.rationale: The columns differ at every dissolved oxygen; compare them row by row.

explanation: Because the experiments differ only in the streambed type, the consistent gap between the two sets of results (higher for gravel bed) shows that the condition affects the number of mayfly nymphs.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Ecologists sampled streams with a range of dissolved-oxygen levels at sites with gravel streambeds, scooping the same area of streambed with a net at each site and counting the mayfly nymphs collected. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated at sites with sandy streambeds, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed with the driver and 300 kg of sandbags aboard

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the steady speed of the car under one condition
choices.rationale: Experiment 1 used a single setting of the load in the car, so by itself it cannot reveal its effect.

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the steady speed of the car was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying speed in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the load in the car
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

explanation: Each experiment holds the load in the car fixed at one setting; the two settings differ between experiments, so comparing Experiments 1 and 2 isolates its effect.

stimulus.title: Speed and Fuel Efficiency
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A test driver drove the same car around a flat track at a steady speed with only the driver aboard for 20 km and measured the fuel used. Fuel efficiency was calculated as kilometers traveled per liter of fuel.
Results (the fuel efficiency): at 60 km/h, 16.5 km/L; at 70 km/h, 17.1 km/L; at 80 km/h, 17.2 km/L; at 90 km/h, 16.9 km/L; at 100 km/h, 16.2 km/L.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated with the driver and 300 kg of sandbags aboard, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 60 km/h, 13.5 km/L; at 70 km/h, 14.0 km/L; at 80 km/h, 14.1 km/L; at 90 km/h, 13.9 km/L; at 100 km/h, 13.3 km/L.

prompt: Which of the following is the most serious flaw in the procedure of Experiment 1?

choices.text: The concentration of the acid was deliberately changed from trial to trial instead of being held constant throughout
choices.rationale: Changing the independent variable is the point of the experiment, not a flaw.

choices.text: The volume of base needed was measured in every trial rather than only in the final trial of the series
choices.rationale: The dependent variable must be measured in every trial.

stimulus.title: Acid Concentration and Titration
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students placed 25 mL of an acid solution of known concentration in a flask with a few drops of indicator and added base solution from a burette, swirling, until the indicator changed color. They recorded the volume of base added. The experimenters did not keep the volume of acid in the flask the same from one trial to the next.
Results (the volume of base needed): at 0.05 mol/L, 6.4 mL; at 0.1 mol/L, 12.8 mL; at 0.15 mol/L, 19.1 mL; at 0.2 mol/L, 25.5 mL; at 0.25 mol/L, 31.9 mL; at 0.3 mol/L, 38.3 mL.

prompt: Based on Experiment 1 alone, which of the following statements goes beyond what the data can support?

choices.text: The mass of soil eroded at 30° was more than twice its value at 10°.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The mass of soil eroded at 30° was more than twice its value at 15°.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The volume of water sprinkled does not affect the mass of soil eroded.
choices.rationale: Correct. The volume of water sprinkled was not varied in Experiment 1, so nothing can be concluded about it.

choices.text: The mass of soil eroded increased with every increase in slope angle.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students filled identical trays with 5 kg of the same soil, tilted each tray to a set angle, and sprinkled water evenly over it from a watering can. They collected the soil that washed out of the tray, dried it, and found its mass. Table 1 lists the results.
